title: Break It Apart: The 7s
goal: I can break 7 into 5 + 2 to find any ×7 fact.

card.desc: Bailey learns to break apart a hard fact: 7 × 6 = (5 × 6) + (2 × 6) = 30 + 12 = 42. She splits real counter arrays with a pencil, learns the 7 × 8 = 56 "5, 6, 7, 8" trick, and spots broken break-aparts. This is the idea behind the area model in Week 3. New words: decompose, addend, distributive, fragment, reassemble, cunning, tactic.

win: You broke the 7s apart and put them back together. Cunning work!

slides.title: Break It Apart on Your Own
slides.text: In class you broke the 7s into 5s and 2s. Now do it on your own. You will type most answers. Finish with Show What You Know.

visual.sub: Two friendly facts make one hard fact.

slides.title: Break, multiply, reassemble
slides.text: Read this once. Then you are ready.

slides.title: Your 7 words
slides.text: Flip each card one more time. Next you will type these words from memory.

words.meaning: to break a number into smaller parts
a number that is added to another number
describes the rule that lets you break a factor apart, multiply each part, and add
a small piece that has broken off something
words.example: Hiccup found a fragment of a dragon eggshell.

words.meaning: to put the pieces of something back together
words.example: The Vikings had to reassemble the broken longship.

words.meaning: clever at planning, especially at tricking others
words.example: The cunning dragon hid behind the rocks to surprise the boys.

words.meaning: a planned move you use to reach a goal
words.example: Breaking 7 into 5 and 2 is a smart tactic.

slides.title: Type the word
slides.text: Type the word that fits. Spell it carefully.

items.q: Which word means to break a number into smaller parts?
items.why: To decompose 7 is to break it into 5 + 2.
items.no: Look back at the word cards. It starts with d.

items.q: Which word means a planned move you use to reach a goal?
items.why: A tactic is a planned move. Breaking 7 into 5 + 2 is a tactic.

items.q: In 40 + 16 = 56, the numbers 40 and 16 are each an ____.
items.why: An addend is a number that is added to another number.
items.no: Which word names a number you add?

items.q: The rule that lets you break a factor apart, multiply each part, and add is the ____ property.
items.no: It starts with d and ends with -tive.

slides.title: Type the missing piece
slides.text: Break the 7 into 5 + 2. Type the missing number.

items.no: The bottom part is 2 groups of 8.
The top part is 5 groups of 6.

slides.title: Correct or broken?
slides.text: Tap a card, then tap the right box. Check both pieces.

items.why: The 2 has to be multiplied too: 2 × 4 = 8. It should be 20 + 8 = 28.

slides.done: A break-apart only works when every piece gets multiplied.

slides.title: Teach someone at home
slides.text: Find someone at home. Teach them for two minutes.
prompts: Show them how to break apart 7 × 6. Draw it if you can.
Tell them about a cunning plan in your book.

slides.title: Sevens on Berk
slides.text: Find the equal groups. Break the 7 apart.

items.q: Toothless sleeps 9 hours each night for 7 nights. How many hours does he sleep?
items.no: 7 equal groups of 9. Break the 7 into 5 + 2.

items.q: The Berk blacksmith has 7 boxes with 6 nails in each box. He uses 12 nails. How many nails are left?
items.no: First find all the nails (7 × 6). Then take away 12.

items.q: The Berk blacksmith has 7 racks with 8 swords on each. Which break-apart finds how many swords?
items.why: Break the 7 racks into 5 + 2. Multiply both by 8: 40 + 16 = 56 swords.
no: The 2 racks have 8 swords each. Multiply the 2 by 8 too.
The first part should be 5 × 8, not 5 × 7.
Each rack has 8 swords. That is equal groups, so multiply.

sets.q: Which break-apart matches 7 × 9?
sets.why: Break 7 into 5 + 2 and multiply both parts by 9.
no: The 2 must be multiplied by 9 too.
That is 7 × 7. The 9 should stay whole.
That only adds. Nothing is multiplied.

sets.q: Hiccup found a fragment of an old map. What did he find?
choices: a small broken piece of the map
sets.why: A fragment is a small piece broken off something.
no: A fragment is only a piece, not the whole thing.
A fragment is one small piece, not a box of maps.
Fragment is about a broken piece, not who drew it.

sets.q: How many days are in 9 weeks?
sets.why: 9 weeks of 7 days is 9 × 7. Turn it around: 7 × 9 = (5 × 9) + (2 × 9) = 45 + 18 = 63 days.
sets.no: Each week has 7 days. 9 groups of 7.

sets.q: Which word means clever at planning, especially at tricking others?
sets.why: Cunning means clever at planning, especially at tricking others.

sets.q: Snotlout says 7 × 6 = 35 + 12 = 47. What is his mistake?
choices: He used 5 × 7 for the first part. It should be 5 × 6 = 30, so 30 + 12 = 42.
sets.why: 7 = 5 + 2, and both parts are multiplied by 6: 30 + 12 = 42.
no: 2 × 6 = 12, so that part is right.
Partial products are added, not subtracted.

sets.q: Bailey splits 7 × 3 into 15 and 6. Then she reassembles them. What does she do?
sets.why: To reassemble is to put the pieces back together. For partial products, that means add: 7 × 3 = 21.
no: 90 is far too big for 7 × 3. Put the pieces together by adding.
Subtracting takes a piece away. Reassemble puts them together.
Every piece is needed to reassemble the whole.

sets.q: Fishlegs packs 7 bags with 8 apples in each bag. He eats 10 apples. How many apples are left?
sets.no: First find all the apples (7 × 8). Then take away 10.

sets.q: Which break-apart matches 7 × 3?
sets.why: Break 7 into 5 + 2 and multiply both parts by 3: 15 + 6 = 21.
no: The 2 must be multiplied by 3 too.
That is 7 × 7 = 49. The 3 should stay whole.
That only adds. Nothing is multiplied.

sets.why: Turn it around: 7 × 8. 5, 6, 7, 8: 56.

sets.q: Which is the best example of a tactic?
choices: Hiccup wants to pass the dragon test.
Hiccup offers Toothless a fish so he will listen.
Hiccup feels nervous before the test.
sets.why: A tactic is a planned move you use to reach a goal. Offering fish is a move Hiccup plans so Toothless will listen.
no: Passing the test is the goal. A tactic is the move you use to reach it.
That describes the dragon. It is not a move.
That is a feeling, not a planned move.

sets.q: How many days are in 6 weeks?
sets.no: Each week has 7 days. 6 groups of 7.

sets.q: Which word means to put the pieces of something back together?
sets.why: To reassemble is to put the pieces back together.

sets.q: Fishlegs says 7 × 9 = 45 + 9 = 54. What is his mistake?
sets.why: Two rows of 9 is 18. 45 + 18 = 63.
no: 45 is 5 × 9, which is right.
Partial products are added.

sets.q: In 45 + 18 = 63, which numbers are the addends?
sets.why: Addends are the numbers you add: 45 and 18.
no: 63 is the sum, the answer.
7 and 9 are the factors of 7 × 9.
5 and 2 are the pieces of the 7, not what you add.

sets.q: Hiccup feeds Toothless 7 fish a day for 6 days. On the last day he adds 5 extra fish. How many fish in all?
sets.no: First find 6 days of 7 fish. Then add the 5 extra.
Turn it around to 7 × 6. Break the 7 into 5 + 2.

sets.q: Which break-apart matches 7 × 8?
sets.why: Break 7 into 5 + 2 and multiply both parts by 8.
no: The 2 must be multiplied by 8 too.
The first part should be 5 × 8, not 5 × 7.
That only adds. Nothing is multiplied.

sets.why: Turn it around: 7 × 9 = 45 + 18 = 63. (Or 70 − 7.)
sets.no: Use a break-apart or ×10 take away one group.

sets.q: Bailey decomposes 7. What does she do?
choices: She puts 5 and 2 together to make 7.
sets.why: To decompose is to break a number into smaller parts.
no: That is multiplying, not breaking apart.
That is putting parts together (reassembling). Decompose is the opposite.
That is the slow road. Decompose means break apart.

sets.q: How many days are in 8 weeks?
sets.no: Each week has 7 days. 8 groups of 7.

sets.q: Which word means a small piece that has broken off something?
sets.why: A fragment is a small broken piece.

sets.q: Snotlout writes 7 × 4 = 20 + 2 = 22. What went wrong?
choices: He never multiplied the 2 by 4. It should be 20 + 8 = 28.
sets.why: Both pieces get multiplied: 2 × 4 = 8. 20 + 8 = 28.
no: 5 × 4 = 20 is right. Look at the second piece.
Partial products are added.

sets.q: Which shows the distributive property?
sets.why: Break a factor apart, multiply each part, and add. That is the distributive property.
no: That switches the factors. That is the commutative property.
That only adds.
That subtracts. Nothing is broken apart.

sets.q: Stoick's 7 ships each carry 9 sheep. 8 sheep jump off. How many sheep are left?
sets.no: First find all the sheep (7 × 9). Then take away 8.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Type most answers. Break the 7 into 5 + 2.

questions.why: Both parts of the 7 get multiplied by 6: 30 + 12 = 42.
no: The 2 must be multiplied by 6 too.
That is 11 × 2 = 22. Break the 7 into 5 and 2, and multiply each piece by 6.

questions.no: Say it: 5, 6, 7, 8. Which number comes after the 7?

questions.q: Which is a way to decompose 7 for multiplying?
questions.why: To decompose is to break into smaller parts. 7 = 5 + 2.
no: 5 × 2 makes 10, not 7. The parts must add up to 7.
7 + 7 doubles the 7. It makes it bigger instead of breaking it apart.
3 + 3 makes 6, not 7. The parts must add up to 7.

questions.q: For 7 × 7, using 7 = 5 + 2, what are the two partial products?
no: 7 is only one seven. The bottom part is 2 sevens.
25 is 5 × 5. The top part is 5 × 7.

questions.q: Stoick's tribe has 7 longships. Each longship has 12 oars. How many oars in all?
questions.why: 7 × 12 = (7 × 10) + (7 × 2) = 70 + 14 = 84. You can break apart the 12 too!

questions.q: Fishlegs practices sword fighting for 3 weeks. How many days is that?
questions.no: Each week has 7 days. 3 groups of 7.

questions.q: Use one of your new words: a sharp ____ of the broken cup cut my finger.
questions.why: A fragment is a small broken piece.
questions.no: Which word means a small broken piece? It starts with f.

choices: Fishlegs wore a warm tactic on his head.
The tactic swam under the boat.
Breaking 7 into 5 and 2 is a smart tactic for hard facts.
questions.why: A tactic is a planned move to reach a goal.
no: A tactic is not something you wear. It is a planned move.
A tactic cannot swim. It is a plan or move.

choices: She used 5 × 7 instead of 5 × 8 for the first part.
no: 16 is already 2 × 8, which is correct. Look at the first part.
7 × 8 is 56. Look at the first partial product.

questions.q: Which is NOT a correct way to find 7 × 6?
questions.why: (5 × 6) + 2 = 32. The 2 was never multiplied by 6. The other two both make 42.
no: This one works: 30 + 12 = 42.
This one works too. It breaks the 6 into 5 + 1: 35 + 7 = 42.

pages.title: Part 1: Break it apart
pages.directions: Break the 7 into 5 + 2. Find both partial products. Then add.

pages.title: Part 2: Split the array
pages.directions: Draw the dots. Draw a line under row 5.

items.text: 6. Above the line: 5 × 8 = ____   Below the line: 2 × 8 = ____   Total: 7 × 8 = ____

pages.title: Part 3: Word power
pages.directions: Use a word from the bank to finish each sentence. Use each word one time.

items.text: 7. Hiccup came up with a ______________ plan to trick the dragon.
8. When I break 7 into 5 + 2, I ______________ the 7.
10. Only a small ______________ of the old map was left.
11. The storm broke the boat, so the Vikings had to ______________ it.
12. My best ______________ for the 8s is double, double, double.
13. The ______________ property lets me break a factor apart.

pages.title: Part 4: Word problems
pages.directions: Show your break-apart. Write the answer with a label.

items.text: 14. The Vikings stack 7 piles of logs. Each pile has 9 logs. How many logs?
15. Hiccup trains Toothless for 7 weeks. How many days is that?

teacher.objective: Bailey finds ×7 facts by decomposing 7 into 5 + 2, finding the two partial products, and adding (7 × 6 = 30 + 12 = 42). She learns 7 × 8 = 56 ("5, 6, 7, 8"), sees that her ×6, ×7 and ×9 shortcuts all use the distributive property, and learns seven new words (decompose, addend, distributive, fragment, reassemble, cunning, tactic).
materials: A pencil or straw to split arrays
7 blank index cards for this lesson's words
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Lesson 3 packet and Lesson 4 packet, printed to send home

plan.do: Class slide 1. Look at her Lesson 3 after-class score together. She tells you what 7 is made of.
Class slide 2. She breaks one of Hiccup's big jobs into steps (sets up today's idea) and names who has changed most.
Class slide 3. She says each double or shortcut out loud before tapping.
Class slides 4–5. Teach the 7 words one at a time; she writes each on an index card. She names the addends in 30 + 12 = 42.
Class slides 6–7. Build 7 rows of 6 counters, pencil under row 5: 30 and 12. Then 7 × 8: 40 and 16. Chant "5, 6, 7, 8."
Class slides 8–9. She writes each break-apart on the whiteboard before tapping; builds 7 piles of 7 and reassembles 35 + 14.
Class slide 10. She says which piece is wrong and what it should be before she types.
Class slides 11–12. Her ×6, ×7 and ×9 shortcuts are all the distributive property (×8 is doubling). Break 7 × 6 both ways; try 7 × 12 and 7 × 11.
Class slide 13. She reads aloud and names the equal groups.
Class slide 14. She teaches 7 × 9 with counters and explains Snotlout's mistake.
Class slide 15. Go through the task list (heavy night: split Tuesday / Wednesday) and hand her the Lesson 3 and 4 packets.

watch: Forgetting to multiply the 2 (7 × 6 = 30 + 2). Point at the bottom 2 rows: "How many are in these two rows?"
Using 5 × 7 for the first part of 7 × 8 (35 + 16). Ask: "Which number did you break apart? Which one stays whole?"
Adding the partial products wrong (45 + 18). Have her use friendly tens: 45 + 15 = 60, then 3 more.
Going back to adding 7 over and over. Say: "That is the long road. Which tactic is shorter?"
"I can't do it." Cover the bottom 2 rows: "Can you do just the 5s part?" One piece at a time.

packet_key.answer: 7 rows of 8 dots with a line under row 5

teacher.notes: Show What You Know is at the end of the After-Class Lesson, done at home tonight; a retake gives a brand-new set of 10. Thursday (Lesson 5) is Prove it with all the 6–9 facts mixed, and you check the Lesson 3 packet and Lesson 4 packet page 1 then. If she scores under 90, start Thursday with the counter array again (7 × 9 and 7 × 7) and have her retake the check before the new lesson.

tasks: Tuesday night: do the After-Class Lesson. Get 90 or more on Show What You Know.
Tuesday night: do the Lesson 3 Practice.
Wednesday: do the Lesson 3 Packet (both pages).
Wednesday: do the Lesson 4 Practice. Aim for 90 or more.
Wednesday: print the Lesson 4 Packet. Do page 1 only. Save page 2 for the weekend.
Tuesday and Wednesday: read How to Train Your Dragon for 15 minutes each day. Find one cunning plan.

slides.title: Break It Apart: The 7s
slides.text: The 7s are tricky because doubling jumps from 4 groups straight to 8 groups and skips 7. So today you use a different tactic: break the 7 into two friendly numbers you already know, 5 and 2.

visual.sub: Two friendly facts make one hard fact.

notes.do: Before you start, look at her Lesson 3 after-class score on the course page. Have about 60 counters (or dried beans), a pencil and the whiteboard ready.
notes.say: "The 7s are tricky because doubling goes 2, 4, 8 and skips right over 7. So today we use a different tactic: break the 7 into two numbers you already know."
notes.ask: "What is 7 made of? Which two numbers would be friendly to multiply by?"
notes.listen: "5 and 2" (or 5 + 2). If she says 3 + 4, accept it as true, then ask which pair has the easier facts.

slides.title: Big problems, smaller pieces
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What happened in the part you read since Monday's lesson?
Think of a big, scary job Hiccup faces. How could he break it into smaller steps? What would step one be?
Which character has changed the most so far? What made them change?
starters: Hiccup could start by … Then he could …

notes.do: 5–7 minutes. Book open to where she stopped.
notes.say: "Big scary jobs are easier in small pieces. That is today's math too."
notes.ask: "Think of a big job Hiccup faces. What would step one be? Step two?" Then: "Who has changed the most so far?"
notes.listen: A real job from the book broken into 2–3 ordered steps, and a character change with a cause ("… changed because …").

items.q: What is 8 × 6? Double three times.
no: Check your last double: 24 + 24 is 48, not 46.
54 is 9 × 6. Three doubles of 6: 12, 24, 48.
42 is 7 × 6. You need 8 groups.

items.q: What is 9 × 5? Use ×10 minus one group.
no: 50 is 10 × 5. Nine groups is one group less, so take away 5.
You took away 9. Take away one group of 5: 50 − 5.
54 is 9 × 6. Start from 50 and take away 5.

items.q: Which word means to cut into two equal parts?
items.why: To halve means to divide by 2. Halve 56 and you get 28.
no: Quadruple means make four times as big.
Amplify means make bigger, louder, or stronger.
Double is the opposite: multiply by 2.

notes.do: She says each double or shortcut out loud before she taps.
notes.ask: "What is the opposite of halve?" "For 9 × 5, which group do you take away?"
notes.listen: "Double." "One group of 5: 50 − 5 = 45." If she misses 8 × 6, have her count the doubles on her fingers again.

slides.title: Seven words for today
slides.text: Jonathan teaches each word. Flip the card, read the meaning, and make your own sentence.

words.meaning: to break a number into smaller parts
a number that is added to another number
describes the rule that lets you break a factor apart, multiply each part, and add
a small piece that has broken off something
words.example: Hiccup found a fragment of a dragon eggshell.

words.meaning: to put the pieces of something back together
words.example: The Vikings had to reassemble the broken longship.

words.meaning: clever at planning, especially at tricking others
words.example: The cunning dragon hid behind the rocks to surprise the boys.

words.meaning: a planned move you use to reach a goal
words.example: Breaking 7 into 5 and 2 is a smart tactic.

notes.do: Teach one word at a time (about 1 minute each). Write each word on an index card for this week's pile.
notes.say: "Decompose means break a number into smaller parts. An addend is a number you add. Distributive is the rule that lets you break a factor apart, multiply each part, and add. A fragment is a broken piece. Reassemble: re- means again, so assemble again, put it back together. Cunning means clever at tricking. A tactic is a planned move to reach a goal."
notes.ask: "In 30 + 12 = 42, what are the addends?" "What is a cunning thing a dragon could do?" "What is one tactic you use when a fact is hard?"
notes.listen: "30 and 12." Book sentences for fragment, cunning and reassemble. For tactic: any real strategy (flip it, double, ×10 take away).

items.q: Bailey decomposes 7 × 8 into 5 × 8 and 2 × 8. Which two addends does she add to get 7 × 8?
no: 35 is 5 × 7. The part is 5 × 8.
5 and 2 are the pieces of the 7. Each piece still has to be multiplied by 8.
56 is the whole answer (the sum). The addends are the two parts you add.

items.q: Which sentence shows a cunning plan?
choices: Snotlout shouted and ran straight at the dragon.
Hiccup left a trail of fish so the dragon would follow it into the cave.
Fishlegs fell asleep during the lesson.
items.why: Cunning means clever at planning or tricking. A fish trail is a sneaky, clever plan.
no: Running straight at a dragon is brave (or silly), but there is no clever plan.
Falling asleep is not a plan at all.

items.q: To put the broken pieces back together is to ____ them. Type the word.
items.why: Reassemble means put the pieces back together.
items.no: re- means again. Which word means put together again?

notes.do: She answers out loud first and explains each wrong choice.
notes.ask: "Why are 5 and 2 not the addends for 7 × 8?"
notes.listen: "They are the pieces of the 7. Each piece still gets multiplied by 8, so the addends are 40 and 16."

slides.title: 7 × 6: break the 7
slides.text: You know your 5s, and ×2 is just a double. So break 7 rows into 5 rows and 2 rows.
slides.tip: The two pieces, 30 and 12, are called partial products. Add them to get the whole product.

notes.do: Hands-on: she builds 7 rows of 6 counters, then lays a pencil under row 5. Reveal each step only after she counts that part.
notes.say: "Above the pencil is a fact you know: 5 × 6. Below the pencil is a double: 2 × 6. Two easy facts make one hard fact."
notes.ask: "How many above the pencil? How many below? How many in all?"
notes.listen: "30 above, 12 below, 42 in all." Have her say "partial products" for 30 and 12.

slides.title: Split the 7 × 8 array
slides.text: Build 7 rows of 8 counters. Lay a pencil under row 5. Count what is above and below the pencil.

steps.text: Above the pencil: 5 rows of 8 = 40. Below the pencil: 2 rows of 8 = 16. In this box picture, the 5 rows are the left box and the 2 rows are the right box.
Here is a trick to remember it. Say the numbers in order: 5, 6, 7, 8.

slides.tip: If you forget the trick, break it apart: 40 + 16 = 56.

notes.do: She builds 7 rows of 8 counters and splits it with the pencil under row 5. Then chant "5, 6, 7, 8" together three times.
notes.ask: "What is above the pencil? Below? Now say the trick: what is 7 × 8?"

no: 47 is 45 + 2. The bottom part is 2 groups of 9, which is 18.
54 is 6 × 9. Add 45 + 18 again.
Check your adding: 45 + 18. 45 + 15 = 60, then 3 more.

items.q: Which break-apart matches 7 × 4?
items.why: Break the 7 into 5 + 2 and multiply both parts by 4: 20 + 8 = 28.
no: The 2 must be multiplied by 4 too. Every piece of the 7 gets multiplied.
That breaks a 7 into 5 + 2 but multiplies by 7. It equals 7 × 7.
That only adds. There is no multiplying at all.

notes.do: Cover the choices. She writes the break-apart on the whiteboard first, then taps.
notes.listen: "The 2 has to be multiplied by 4 too. Every piece gets multiplied."

slides.title: Hiccup's shield piles
slides.text: Hiccup stacks 7 piles of shields. Each pile has 7 shields. Build the piles.
slides.why: 7 piles of 7. The first 5 piles: 5 × 7 = 35. The last 2 piles: 2 × 7 = 14. Reassemble: 35 + 14 = 49.
slides.hint: How many piles? How many shields in each pile?

notes.do: She builds 7 piles of 7 on screen, and 7 piles of 7 counters on the table. Slide the pencil between pile 5 and pile 6.
notes.ask: "How many in the first 5 piles? In the last 2 piles? Reassemble them."

slides.title: Check the break-aparts
slides.text: Say which piece you checked. Then type correct or broken.

items.q: 7 × 3 = 15 + 6. Is this break-apart correct or broken? Type correct or broken.
7 × 6 = 30 + 2. Is this break-apart correct or broken? Type correct or broken.
items.why: The 2 was never multiplied. It should be 30 + 12. Broken.

items.q: 7 × 8 = 35 + 16. Is this break-apart correct or broken? Type correct or broken.
items.why: 35 is 5 × 7, not 5 × 8. It should be 40 + 16. Broken.

items.q: 7 × 7 = 35 + 7. Is this break-apart correct or broken? Type correct or broken.
items.why: The bottom part is 2 sevens, which is 14. It should be 35 + 14. Broken.
items.no: How many sevens are in the bottom part?

notes.do: Before she types, she must say WHICH piece is wrong and what it should be.
notes.ask: "Which piece was not multiplied? What should it be?"
notes.listen: "The 2 was not multiplied by 6. It should be 12."

slides.title: You have been breaking apart all along
slides.text: Breaking a factor into friendly parts, multiplying each part, then putting them back together is called the distributive property. Your ×6, ×7 and ×9 shortcuts all use it.

visual.text:
×6 → 6 = 5 + 1  →  5 groups + 1 more group
×7 → 7 = 5 + 2  →  5 groups + 2 more groups
×9 → 9 = 10 − 1  →  10 groups − 1 group

slides.tip: Your ×8 tool is different: it doubles three times. Keep both kinds of tools.

notes.do: Point at each line and have her say the tool in her own words.
notes.say: "Your 6s, 7s and 9s shortcuts are the same big idea: break a factor into friendly parts, multiply each part, put them back together."
notes.ask: "Which tool breaks 6 apart? Which one breaks 9 apart with a take-away? Is the ×8 tool a break-apart?"
notes.listen: "6 is 5 + 1." "9 is 10 − 1." "No, ×8 is doubling three times."

slides.title: You can break either factor
slides.text: The distributive property works on either factor. Pick the one that gives the friendliest parts.
slides.tip: Next week you use this on numbers like 75 × 8. Today's tactic is the key.

notes.do: Write 7 × 6 both ways on the whiteboard side by side. Then try 7 × 11 together: (7 × 10) + (7 × 1).
notes.ask: "Which way was easier for you? What is 7 × 11?"

items.q: A week has 7 days. Toothless eats 8 fish every day. How many fish does he eat in one week?
no: 15 is 7 + 8. He eats 8 fish on each of 7 days, so multiply.
54 is 6 × 9. Break it apart: 40 + 16.
48 is 6 × 8. A week has 7 days, not 6.

items.q: Hiccup trains Toothless for 4 weeks. How many days is that?
no: 11 is 4 + 7. Each week has 7 days, so these are equal groups.
24 is 4 × 6. A week has 7 days.
21 is only 3 weeks. Add one more week of 7.

notes.do: She reads each problem aloud and names the equal groups before tapping.
notes.listen: "Every week has the same number of days: 7."

slides.title: Teach it back
slides.text: Now you are the teacher. Explain it to Jonathan.
prompts: Teach me 7 × 9 with a break-apart. Name the partial products.
Snotlout wrote 7 × 6 = 30 + 2. Explain his mistake like a teacher would.
Tell me about a cunning plan in your book. Was it a good tactic?

notes.do: She uses the counters or the whiteboard to show her answer.
notes.listen: "45 and 18 are the partial products; 45 + 18 = 63." "He didn't multiply the 2 by 6." A real plan from the book with a reason.

slides.title: Break it, then reassemble it
slides.text: Today you learned ×7 = ×5 + ×2, the 5, 6, 7, 8 trick, and that your 6s, 7s and 9s shortcuts all use the distributive property.
